newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israeli stock market indifferent to budget.
newsitem.headline: Israeli stock market indifferent to budget.

text.p: Israeli shares opened slightly higher on Thursday with the market little affected by parliament's preliminary approval of the 1997 budget after trading hours on Wednesday, traders said.
The benchmark Mishtanim Index of top 100 shares rose 0.46 percent or 0.85 points to 187.18 while the Maof 25 blue-chip index gained 0.37 percent to 197.63.
"There is no reaction to what happened. There is a continued lack of interest on the bourse and turnover is very thin," said Amit Goldwasser, investment manager at Nesuah Trading.
Shahar Gazit, a trader at Batucha Securities, attributed this morning's gains to the strength of bond prices and the higher dollar against the shekel, which helps exporters' profits.
The dollar was trading up at 3.270 shekels against 3.267 on Wednesday.
"It's positive that the budget was passed on the first reading but a lot can still happen until the second and third readings (in late December)," Gazit said.

Gesher, a faction in the ruling Likud party led by Foreign Minister David Levy, dropped its opposition to the legislation in return for a letter from Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu promising to consider changes in the budget before a final vote in parliament by year's end.

The 190.8 billion shekel budget, which includes 4.9 billion shekels in spending cuts, is being challenged by coalition members who say it hurts lower-income groups. The budget would reduce subsidies for health care and child allowances.

Goldwasser said there was concern in the market that the letter could result in the government cutting less than 4.9 billion shekels although Netanyahu said on Wednesday he was committed to preserving the framework of the budget.
Goldwasser said the market was hoping for cuts beyond the 4.9 billion shekels, which would allow the central bank to reduce interest rates.
Given the extremely thin turnover of recent days, traders said it was difficult to determine the market's true direction.
